summary: Details how labels are distributed to and from ATM label switching routers using LDP when routes come from ordinary network-layer routing. It extends and clarifies RFC 3031 and RFC 3036. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary:
An ATM switch already swaps short identifiers between incoming and outgoing channels. RFC 3035 makes those identifiers into MPLS labels, so an ATM switch can act as a label switching router while using ordinary IP routing to decide where traffic should go.

Because the labels sit in the cell header, some normal MPLS machinery has to change. A small shim header has to be added, the time-to-live has to be carried across the ATM cloud, and the label distribution protocol has to hand out labels on demand with a hop count attached.

questions: how does mpls work over atm
how is ttl handled in mpls over atm
subtitle: How ATM switches become MPLS label switching routers, and how labels are handed out.

tldr.problem: MPLS lets routers forward packets on a label instead of looking up every destination in a table. ATM switches were built to do exactly that kind of label swapping, but they had no way to receive labels, and their hardware rules out several things a normal MPLS router takes for granted.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3035 defines an ATM label switching router, which runs ordinary network layer routing and carries its label in the VPI and VCI fields of the ATM cell header. Labels are distributed with LDP using the downstream-on-demand technique, with a hop count that also serves as a loop detector.
tldr.outcome: The document is a Proposed Standard from January 2001 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It extends and clarifies the MPLS Architecture and the LDP specification, and it leaves multicast, explicitly routed paths and virtual path merging out of scope.

facts.label: Reserved VCI range
facts.value: A VCI in the range 0 to 32 must not be used as a label

today: RFC 3035 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2001. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It extends and clarifies the MPLS Architecture and the LDP specification for the case of ATM switches used as label switching routers, and it leaves multicast, explicitly routed paths and virtual path merging outside its scope.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The MPLS Architecture discusses the way in which ATM switches may be used as Label Switching Routers. The ATM switches run network layer routing algorithms such as OSPF and IS-IS, and their data forwarding is based on the results of those algorithms. No ATM-specific routing or addressing is needed. ATM switches used in this way are known as ATM-LSRs.

This document extends and clarifies the relevant portions of the MPLS Architecture and the LDP specification by setting out in more detail the procedures used when distributing labels to or from ATM-LSRs, when those labels represent Forwarding Equivalence Classes for which the routes are determined on a hop-by-hop basis by network layer routing algorithms. The label distribution technique described here is the one the MPLS Architecture calls downstream-on-demand. It must be used by ATM-LSRs that are not capable of VC merge, and is optional for ATM-LSRs that are capable of it.

The document does not specify the label distribution techniques to be used where the routes are explicitly chosen before label distribution begins, where the routes are intended to diverge from the conventional hop-by-hop routes, where the labels represent FECs that consist of multicast packets, or where the LSRs use VP merge. Further statements made about ATM-LSR label distribution do not necessarily apply in these cases.

The document also specifies the MPLS encapsulation to be used when sending labeled packets to or from ATM-LSRs, and in that respect it is a companion to the MPLS Label Stack Encoding specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The scope is narrow on purpose. This is about ATM switches doing plain IP routing hop by hop, with labels handed out as each switch needs them.

sections.title: Definitions and the Limits of ATM Hardware
sections.content:
A Label Switching Router is a device which implements the label switching control and forwarding components. A label switching controlled ATM interface, or LC-ATM interface, is an ATM interface controlled by the label switching control component. When a packet traversing such an interface is received, it is treated as a labeled packet, and the packet's top label is inferred either from the contents of the VCI field or from the combined contents of the VPI and VCI fields. Any two LDP peers connected via an LC-ATM interface use LDP negotiations to determine which of these cases applies to that interface.

An ATM-LSR is a LSR with a number of LC-ATM interfaces which forwards cells between these interfaces, using labels carried in the VCI or VPI/VCI field, without reassembling the cells into frames before forwarding. A frame-based LSR forwards complete frames between its interfaces, and may have zero, one or more LC-ATM interfaces. Sometimes a single box behaves as an ATM-LSR with respect to certain pairs of interfaces and as a frame-based LSR with respect to others, for example an ATM switch with an ethernet interface; the two functions can be considered as coresident in one box. An LC-ATM interface is intended to connect two ATM-LSRs, or to connect an ATM-LSR to a frame-based LSR. Connecting two frame-based LSRs with one is not considered in the document.

An ATM-LSR domain is a set of ATM-LSRs which are mutually interconnected by LC-ATM interfaces. The Edge Set of such a domain is the set of frame-based LSRs connected to members of the domain by LC-ATM interfaces, and a frame-based LSR in an edge set may be called an Edge LSR. VC-merge is the process by which a switch receives cells on several incoming VCIs and transmits them on a single outgoing VCI without causing the cells of different AAL5 PDUs to become interleaved.

While the MPLS architecture permits considerable flexibility in LSR implementation, an ATM-LSR is constrained by the capabilities of the possibly pre-existing hardware and by the restrictions on cell format imposed by the ATM standards. Three features of ATM switches matter. The label swapping function is performed on fields, the VCI and or VPI, in the cell header, which dictates the size and placement of the labels in a packet. Multipoint-to-point and multipoint-to-multipoint virtual circuits are generally not supported, so most switches cannot support VC merge. And there is generally no capability to perform a TTL-decrement function as is performed on IP headers in routers.
sections.plainLanguage: Three hardware facts shape everything that follows. The label has to live in the cell header, because that is where an ATM switch swaps identifiers. Most ATM switches cannot merge several incoming channels into one. And ATM switches do not normally decrement a time-to-live field.

sections.title: Use of VPI and VCIs
sections.content:
Label switching is accomplished by associating labels with Forwarding Equivalence Classes and using the label value to forward packets, including determining the value of any replacement label. In an ATM-LSR, the label is carried in the VPI/VCI field, or, when two ATM-LSRs are connected via an ATM Virtual Path, in the VCI field. Labeled packets must be transmitted using the null encapsulation defined in RFC 2684.

In addition, if two LDP peers are connected via an LC-ATM interface, a non-MPLS connection capable of carrying unlabelled IP packets must be available. This connection is used to carry LDP packets between the two peers, and may also be used for other unlabeled packets. The LLC/SNAP encapsulation of RFC 2684 must be used on it. It should be possible to configure an LC-ATM interface with additional VPI/VCIs used to carry control information or non-labelled packets, and in that case the VCI values must not be in the 0 to 32 range. These may use either the null encapsulation or the LLC/SNAP encapsulation.

Two LSRs are said to be directly connected over an LC-ATM interface if all cells transmitted out that interface by one LSR will reach the other, and there are no ATM switches between the two. When two LSRs are directly connected via an LC-ATM interface, they jointly control the allocation of VPI/VCIs on the interface, and they may agree to use the VPI/VCI field to encode a single label. The default VPI/VCI value for the non-MPLS connection is VPI 0 and VCI 32. Other values can be configured, as long as both parties are aware of the configured value. A VPI/VCI value whose VCI part is in the range 0 to 32 inclusive must not be used as the encoding of a label. With the exception of these reserved values, the VPI/VCI values used in the two directions of the link may be treated as independent spaces. The allowable ranges of VCIs are communicated through LDP.

It can sometimes be useful to treat two LSRs as adjacent in some LSP across an LC-ATM interface even though the connection between them is made through an ATM cloud via an ATM Virtual Path. In that case the VPI field is not available to MPLS and the label must be encoded entirely within the VCI field. The default VCI value of the non-MPLS connection between the LSRs is 32, the VPI is set to whatever is required to make use of the Virtual Path, and the same 0 to 32 reservation applies. The allowable ranges of VPI/VCIs are communicated through LDP, and if more than one VPI is used for label switching the allowable range of VCIs may be different for each VPI.

It may also be useful to treat two LSRs as adjacent across an LC-ATM interface even though the connection between them is made through an ATM cloud via a set of ATM Switched Virtual Circuits. The current document does not specify the procedure for handling this case. The procedures allow a VCID to be assigned to each such VC and specify how LDP can be used to bind a VCID to a FEC; the top label of a received packet would then be inferred, through a one-to-one mapping, from the virtual circuit on which the packet arrived, and there would not be a default VPI or VCI value for the non-MPLS connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Two numbers identify an ATM channel: the virtual path identifier and the virtual channel identifier. The label goes in one or both of them, depending on how the link is built. Numbers 0 to 32 in the channel identifier are kept for the control connection that carries LDP itself.

sections.title: Label Distribution and Maintenance Procedures
sections.content:
The document uses downstream-on-demand label distribution. These procedures must be used by ATM-LSRs that do not support VC merge, and may also be used by those that do. The behavior of members of the edge set of an ATM-LSR domain is described first, since these edge LSRs are not themselves ATM-LSRs and their behavior is the same whether the domain contains VC-merge capable LSRs or not.

Consider a member of the edge set. Assume that, as a result of its routing calculations, it selects an ATM-LSR as the next hop of a certain FEC, and that the next hop is reachable via a LC-ATM interface. The Edge LSR uses LDP to request a label binding for that FEC from the next hop, with the hop count field set to 1. If the Edge LSR's previous hop is using downstream-on-demand distribution to ask the Edge LSR for a label and is not merging the LSP with any other, and the request from the previous hop has a hop count of h, then the hop count in the request issued by the Edge LSR should be h+1 rather than 1. Once the Edge LSR receives the binding information it may use MPLS forwarding procedures to transmit packets in the FEC, using the specified label as the outgoing label. If a hop count is associated with the binding, the ATM-LSR should adjust a data packet's TTL by this amount before transmitting it, and in any event it must adjust the TTL by at least one. When an edge LSR receives a label binding request from an ATM-LSR, it allocates a label and returns a binding containing the allocated label to the peer that asked, setting the hop count to 1. When a routing calculation causes an Edge LSR to change the next hop for a FEC and the former next hop was in the ATM-LSR domain, the Edge LSR should notify the former next hop that the binding is no longer needed.

When an ATM-LSR receives a label binding request for a certain FEC from a peer connected over a LC-ATM interface, it allocates a label, requests a label binding from the next hop for that FEC, and returns a binding containing the allocated incoming label back to the peer that asked. The document defines a maximum hop count value, MAXHOP, whose default is 255 but which may be configured differently. The hop count in the request the ATM-LSR sends must be set to one more than the hop count in the request it received. If the resulting hop count exceeds MAXHOP, the request must not be sent to the next hop and the ATM-LSR must notify the upstream neighbour that its request cannot be satisfied.

The ATM-LSR may wait for the request to be satisfied from downstream before returning the binding upstream, a form of ingress-initiated ordered control. In that case, as long as the ATM-LSR receives from downstream a hop count greater than 0 and less than MAXHOP, it must increment that count and include the result in the binding it returns upstream; if the count exceeds MAXHOP, a binding must not be passed upstream and the upstream peer must be told the request cannot be satisfied; if the count received from downstream is 0, the count passed upstream should also be 0, indicating that the actual hop count is unknown. Alternatively the ATM-LSR may return the binding upstream without waiting, independent control, specifying a hop count of 0.

An ATM-LSR or edge set member may receive multiple binding requests for the same FEC from the same ATM-LSR. It must generate a new binding for each request and retain any existing bindings, and for each request received it must also generate a new binding request toward the next hop. When a routing calculation causes a change of next hop, the ATM-LSR must notify the former next hop that the binding is no longer needed. When a LSR receives such a notification it may deallocate the label and destroy the binding; if it does destroy the binding, it must notify the next hop for the FEC, and it may only re-use a binding if it receives a request for the same FEC with the same hop count as the request that originally created it.

When a route changes, the label bindings are re-established from the point where the route diverges from the previous route, and LSRs upstream of that point are, with one exception, oblivious to the change. Whenever an LSR changes its next hop for a FEC and the new next hop is reachable via a LC-ATM interface, it must request a new label binding from the new next hop for each label it has bound to that FEC and distributed upstream. If the hop count in a new binding from downstream differs from the count previously conveyed upstream, the ATM-LSR must notify the upstream neighbour of the change, and each ATM-LSR in turn must increment the count and pass it upstream until it reaches the ingress Edge LSR. If at any point the count equals MAXHOP, the ATM-LSR should withdraw the binding from the upstream neighbour. A hop count of 0 must be passed upstream unchanged. If a request to the next hop is not satisfied, the ATM-LSR should destroy the binding it created and notify the requester, and if an ATM-LSR receives a request with a hop count exceeding MAXHOP it must not establish a binding and must return an error. When a LSR loses its LDP session with another LSR, binding information learned via that connection must be discarded. An ATM-LSR should use split-horizon when it satisfies binding requests from its neighbours. Non-merging ATM-LSRs would generally use conservative label retention mode.

Relatively minor changes are needed for VC-merge-capable ATM-LSRs. The primary difference is that such a switch needs only one outgoing label per FEC, even if multiple requests for bindings arrive from upstream neighbours. When it receives a binding request and does not already have an outgoing label binding for that FEC, or an outstanding request for one, it must issue a bind request to its next hop as it would if it were not merge-capable. If it already has an outgoing binding, it does not need to issue a downstream request; it may simply allocate an incoming label and return it, and when packets with that label as top label arrive, the top label value is replaced with the existing outgoing label for the same FEC. When sending a binding upstream, the hop count of the downstream binding must be incremented by 1, with the exceptions that a hop count of 0 must be passed unchanged and a count already at MAXHOP must not be passed upstream, an error being sent instead. A merge-capable ATM-LSR must still issue a new binding every time it receives a request from upstream, since switches upstream may not support VC merge, but it only issues a corresponding downstream request if it does not already have a binding for the route.
sections.plainLanguage:
Labels are not announced in advance. Each switch asks its next hop for a label when it needs one, passes the request on with the hop count raised by one, and answers the requester with the label it allocated for incoming traffic.

The hop count does double duty: it measures how many ATM switches the packet will cross, and it detects loops. A switch that would push the count past MAXHOP refuses the request instead of passing it on.

sections.title: Encapsulation
sections.content:
The procedures in this section affect only the Edge LSRs of the ATM-LSR domain; the ATM-LSRs themselves do not modify the encapsulation in any way. Labeled packets must be transmitted using the null encapsulation of RFC 2684.

Except in certain circumstances, when a labeled packet is transmitted on an LC-ATM interface where the VPI/VCI or VCID is interpreted as the top label in the label stack, the packet must also contain a shim header. If the packet has a label stack with n entries, it must carry a shim with n entries. The actual value of the top label is encoded in the VPI/VCI field. The label value of the top entry in the shim, which is just a placeholder entry, must be set to 0 upon transmission and must be ignored upon reception. The packet's outgoing TTL and its CoS are carried in the TTL and CoS fields respectively of the top stack entry in the shim.

If a packet has a label stack with only one entry, it still requires a single-entry shim of 4 bytes, even though the actual label value is encoded into the VPI/VCI field. This is done so that the packet always has a shim, since otherwise there would be no way to tell whether it had one, and so no way to know whether there are additional label stack entries.

The only ways to eliminate this extra overhead are through apriori knowledge that packets have only a single label, for example where the network only supports one level of label, or by using two VCs per FEC, one for packets with a single label and one for packets with more than one label. The second technique would require a way of signalling via LDP that the VC carries only packets with a single label, and when supporting VC merge one would also have to take care not to merge a VC on which the shim is not used into a VC on which it is used, or the reverse. While either technique is permitted, it is doubtful that they have any practical utility. If the shim header is not present, the outgoing TTL is carried in the TTL field of the network layer header.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the real label is stored in the channel identifier, the label stack still needs a small header to carry the rest of the stack, the TTL and the class of service. Even a packet with a single label carries one, so that a receiver can tell whether more labels follow.

sections.title: TTL Manipulation
sections.content:
The procedures in this section affect only the Edge LSRs of the ATM-LSR domain; the ATM-LSRs themselves do not modify the TTL in any way.

If a packet was received by the Edge LSR as an unlabeled packet, the incoming TTL comes from the IP header. If a packet was received as a labeled packet, using the encapsulation specified in the MPLS Label Stack Encoding specification, the incoming TTL comes from the entry at the top of the label stack.

If a hop count has been associated with the label binding used when the packet is forwarded, the outgoing TTL is set to the larger of zero or the difference between the incoming TTL and the hop count. If a hop count has not been associated with the binding, the outgoing TTL is set to the larger of zero or one less than the incoming TTL.

If this causes the outgoing TTL to become zero, the packet must not be transmitted as a labeled packet using the specified label. It may be treated as having expired, which may cause an ICMP message to be transmitted, or it may be forwarded as an unlabeled packet with a TTL one less than the incoming TTL, which would need to be done over a non-MPLS connection. If the incoming TTL is 1, only the first of these options applies. If the packet is forwarded as a labeled packet, the outgoing TTL is carried as specified in the encapsulation section.

When an Edge LSR receives a labeled packet over an LC-ATM interface, it obtains the incoming TTL from the top label stack entry of the generic encapsulation, or, if that encapsulation is not present, from the IP header. If the packet's next hop is an ATM-LSR, the outgoing TTL is formed using the procedures described here; otherwise it is formed using the procedures in the MPLS Label Stack Encoding specification. The procedures are intended to apply only to unicast packets.
sections.plainLanguage: An ATM switch does not normally reduce a time-to-live, so the edge router has to do it for the whole ATM domain. It subtracts the hop count of the binding, which is how many ATM switches the packet will cross, and it drops the packet if the result reaches zero.

sections.title: Optional Loop Detection with Path Vectors
sections.content:
Every ATM-LSR must implement, as a configurable option, a procedure for detecting forwarding loops, referred to as the LDPV procedure. This procedure does not prevent the formation of forwarding loops, but does ensure that any such loops are detected. If the option is not enabled, loops are detected by the hop count mechanism. If it is enabled, loops are detected more quickly, but at a higher cost in overhead.

When an LSR R sends a request for a label binding to its next hop, and R does not support VC merging and is configured to use LDPV, then if R is sending the request because it is an ingress node for that LSP or because it has acquired a new next hop, R must include a path vector object with the request, and the path vector object must contain only R's own address. If R is sending the request as a result of having received a request from an upstream LSR, then if the received request has a path vector object, R must add its own address to it and pass the result to its next hop; if the received request does not have one, R must include a path vector object containing only its own address. An LSR which supports VC merge should not include a path vector object in the requests it sends. If an LSR receives a label binding request whose path vector object contains the address of the node itself, it concludes that the label binding requests have travelled in a loop and must act as it would in the case where the hop count exceeds MAXHOP.

Upstream, the path vector object is included in a label binding response message when the LSR is configured for LDPV, supports VC merge, is not the egress for the LSP, and is not informing its neighbours of a decrease in the hop count. If the change in hop count came from the next hop and that message included a path vector object, the LSR must add itself to the object and pass the result upstream; otherwise it must create a new object with only its own address. An LSR which supports VC merge may include a path vector object in any label binding response message it sends upstream, and in particular may respond to its upstream neighbours with the path vector object formed by adding its own address to a received path vector. If an LSR does not support VC merge it should not send a path vector object upstream. If an LSR receives a message from its next hop with a path vector object containing its own address, it must act as it would if it had received a message with a hop count equal to MAXHOP. LSRs configured for LDPV should not store a path vector once the corresponding path vector object has been transmitted.

If the ATM-LSR domain consists entirely of non-merging ATM-LSRs, path vectors need never be sent upstream, since any loops will be detected by means of the path vectors travelling downstream. By not sending path vectors unless the hop count increases, they are not sent in many situations where there is no loop; the cost is that in some situations where there is a loop, the time taken to detect it may be longer.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a faster way to spot a loop than counting hops. Each switch puts its own address into a list and passes the list along. If a switch sees its own address in the list, it knows the request has gone round in a circle.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The encapsulation and procedures specified in this document do not interfere in any way with the application of authentication or encryption to network layer packets, such as the application of IPSEC to IP datagrams.

The procedures do not protect against the alteration, whether accidental or malicious, of MPLS labels, and such alteration could cause misforwarding. They also do not enable a receiving LSR to authenticate the transmitting LSR. A discussion of the security considerations applicable to the label distribution mechanism is in the LDP specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here changes how a packet is authenticated or encrypted. But the labels themselves are not protected, so an attacker who can rewrite them can send traffic the wrong way.

viz.caption: How an ATM switch acts as a label switching router

layers.label: Network layer routing
layers.detail: OSPF, IS-IS and other routing protocols decide the route hop by hop

layers.label: Label switching control
layers.detail: LDP allocates, distributes and maintains the label bindings

layers.label: ATM forwarding
layers.detail: The switch swaps labels in the VPI and VCI fields of the cell header

viz.caption: Where the label goes in each kind of ATM connection

cells: The VPI/VCI field may encode a single label
Entirely in the VCI field, because the VPI is not available to MPLS
A VCID is assigned to each VC and the top label is inferred from the circuit the packet arrived on
No default VPI or VCI value

viz.caption: What a non-merge ATM switch does with a label request

items.title: Allocate a label
items.text: The switch allocates an incoming label for the flow it has been asked about.

items.title: Ask the next hop
items.text: It requests a binding from the next hop, setting the hop count to one more than the count in the request it received.

items.title: Answer the requester
items.text: It returns a binding containing the allocated incoming label to the peer that asked.

items.title: Respect MAXHOP
items.text: If the resulting hop count exceeds MAXHOP, the request is not sent downstream and the upstream neighbour is told the request cannot be satisfied.

cells: Always sent to the next hop
Only sent when there is no outgoing binding and no outstanding request
Must notify the former next hop that the binding is no longer needed
May optionally release the binding from the former next hop
A binding for every request received
Still a new binding for every request, since upstream switches may not merge

viz.caption: What the edge router puts on the wire

items.title: Null encapsulation
items.text: Labeled packets must be transmitted using the null encapsulation defined in RFC 2684.

items.title: A shim is always present
items.text: Except in certain circumstances, a labeled packet on an LC-ATM interface must also carry a shim header, with one entry for each label in the stack.

items.title: The top label lives in the VPI/VCI
items.text: The real value of the top label is encoded in the VPI/VCI field. The label value in the top entry of the shim is set to 0 on transmission and ignored on reception.

items.title: TTL and CoS ride in the shim
items.text: The outgoing TTL and the class of service are carried in the TTL and CoS fields of the top stack entry in the shim.

items.title: One label still needs a shim
items.text: A packet with a single label still carries a single-entry shim of 4 bytes, so that a receiver can tell whether more entries follow.
